intent: Replace the families players try and abandon with lineages they return to, without changing the shape of any circuit. A family is judged on four measured signals, all re-derived by tools/funAudit.ts into data/fun_audit.json: replay (KovaaK's plays per player), reach (players on its Novice and Intermediate rungs), consensus (how many benchmarks evxl lists use any of its rungs) and local run-to-run noise. Replay is the strongest signal of a scenario people enjoy; noise matters because a delta-scored match on a noisy scenario is decided by luck.

families.isolates: Fast, clean flicks between small static targets on one wall.
families.why: 1wall 6targets small is the most played scenario on KovaaK's after the sandbox intro, 1.29 million players at 57 plays each, and the season had no member of its lineage. Jumbo introduces it, TE is the standard, small and extra small tighten the target without changing the rhythm.

families.isolates: Short snaps to spheres in a narrow field of view.
families.why: 5 Sphere Hipfire is a long-standing micro-flick staple; the Small edit alone has half a million players. The four rungs are one scenario at four target sizes, so the difficulty order is the author's own.

families.isolates: Rhythm clicking on a steady stream of tiles, fast feedback on every shot.
families.why: Tile Frenzy is the scenario players describe as satisfying even when they concede it is easy, which is exactly the Novice job. Jumbo and standard carry the rhythm; Mini moves the wall far away so the same rhythm needs small movements; Extra mini is the smallest edit on a real board.

families.isolates: One-wall target selection with ammo that reloads on kill instead of accuracy scoring.
families.why: 1w4ts Voltaic is named by four benchmarks and replayed 28.5 times per player, and the reload edits it grew are replayed nearly as often. The rungs step from larger targets through the Voltaic cut to the reload edits at smaller sizes.

families.isolates: Three small static targets in a small range of motion: fingertip precision.
families.why: The previous Micro family had Novice and Intermediate leaderboards of 175 and 532 entries. RawMouseControlClicking3 is replayed 51.6 times per player, among the highest on KovaaK's. Reload Easy is 25% bigger, Reload removes accuracy scoring, Clicking3 restores it, and 30% smaller tightens it.

families.isolates: Reading dodging targets on one wall and clicking at the moment they settle.
families.why: Keeps Pasu in the circuit on the lineage players actually play: its Novice and Intermediate rungs have about thirty-five times the players of the Pasu rungs they replace (fun_audit.json reach). Slow introduces it, small halves the target, and the reactive edit makes the small targets react. The Reload edit, which more benchmarks name, is left out because it runs 86 seconds (50 local runs, 84% agreement in scenario_durations.json).

families.isolates: Short dynamic micro-flicks between two bots, a hybrid of microshot, reflex flick and Pasu.
families.why: Trims the circuit's Pasu-style families from four to three, the source of most complaints about luck deciding a run. Tamspeed's author publishes the ladder as named tiers, so the order is his.

families.isolates: Clicking linearly moving heads on time, with ammo refilled on kill.
families.why: Floating Heads Timing 400% is the original the Floating Heads family was built from; its Novice and Intermediate rungs have eight times the players and more than twice the replay of the family it replaces. Larger introduces it; FIXED removes a frame-rate speed inconsistency and locks field of view; Extra Small Speed shrinks the head and speeds it up. The FIXED Extra Small edit was the natural Expert rung but its board is under the floor the Expert window sets for a board its ranks are cut from.
rungs: Floating Heads Timing Extra Small Speed

families.isolates: Single-click bots leaping in arcs and changing depth.
families.why: Adds arcing movement the circuit lacked and replaces one of its least replayed families. Voltaic's own tiers set the order; the Expert rung is the 20% smaller edit of Advanced.

families.isolates: Keeping a dot centred through semi-predictable strafes inside a small cage.
families.why: cloverRawControl is named by eleven benchmarks, tied for the most of any scenario the season did not use, and its Easy edit by nine more. The previous PreciseTrack family started on a 293-entry leaderboard. Big, Easy and standard are the author's own steps; Expert is Viscose's hard edit, used because the author's Hard board is under the floor the Expert window sets.

families.isolates: Pure smoothness against a strafing bot, with glass walls giving time to react.
families.why: SYW FIXED is replayed 47.6 times per player, one of the highest rates of any tracking scenario on KovaaK's. Easy and the original lock field of view; FIXED forces ADS to remove the cheese; Extra thin narrows the bot.
rungs: SYW (Smooth Your Wrist) FIXED Extra thin

families.isolates: Smooth, precise tracking of a bot moving along curved walls.
families.why: PGTI is named by ten benchmarks and comes up again and again in community lists of favourite tracking scenarios. Easy 80% slows the Easy cut; Slower 80% slows the standard one; the standard edit is last. The Gold edit is left out because its bot is enlarged from Easy, which would put an easier scenario above a harder one.

families.isolates: Reacting to long strafes, moving closer with every rung so the angular speed grows.
families.why: The long-strafes lineage carries some of the highest replay in tracking. The ladder moves the bot from kinda far to midrange to close, then thins it, so difficulty grows along one visible axis.
rungs: Close long strafes invincible very thin

families.isolates: Following an airborne bot's small, sharp dodges without overcorrecting.
families.why: Same skill, rebuilt on the Air Angelic 4 lineage whose Easy edit nine benchmarks use. The previous Novice and Intermediate rungs had leaderboards of 798 and 1,637 entries. The steps go from 80% speed to Easy, the standard edit, then the smaller bot.

families.isolates: Small, fast switches between close targets: 1w2t smallflicks crossed with voxTS.
families.why: Wave Relay had the lowest replay in the season, under three plays per player. beanTS is named by eight benchmarks and has a board of over nine thousand players at every rung. Larger, standard and 30% smaller are target sizes; 200% doubles the speed.

families.isolates: Switching between heads with no bodies and no reload across a wide field.
families.why: A long-standing switching classic whose NR edit six benchmarks name, with about twice the Novice and Intermediate players of PivoTS. Easy, standard and small are the author's sizes; Speed lowers time-to-kill and enlarges the heads for pure pace.

families.isolates: Flick then track: kill dodging bots and transfer cleanly to the next.
families.why: Floatswitch was the least replayed evasive family. patTargetSwitch is the original flick-and-track switching scenario and is not Voltaic, which keeps the Voltaic share of this category from growing. The Expert rung plays the same task while moving through a 360 room.

families.isolates: Tracking fast arcing skeets and transferring to the next as each one breaks.
families.why: Hop Transfer was the second least replayed evasive family. Skeet Tracking has 386 thousand players at 31 plays each. 85% Speed slows it for Novice; Goated and Goated Small are the published harder edits.

rungs.why: The Novice rung had 225 players on its board. Wide Wall 6Targets is the classic six-target wide wall, the natural entry to the ww4t and Wide Wall 3 rungs above it.
The Novice rung had 441 players on its board. Voltaic's own Novice cut is the same scenario as the DotTS rungs above it.
